error_modes.label: Altitude control in straight and level flight and in turns

texts.0: SP, due to pitch attitude set by outside reference alone and never confirmed on the altimeter, did not hold the assigned altitude in straight and level flight and in turns up to 60 degrees of bank. The nose was allowed to drop at each turn entry and the excursion built to about 450 feet, well beyond the 300 foot limit, with the trend still developing. IP had to intervene on the controls to return the aircraft to the assigned altitude.
texts.1: SP applied insufficient back pressure at turn entry and did not re-establish the pitch attitude with a positive elevator input. The altitude deviation reached 300 feet, at the limit of the standard, and was arrested only after repeated verbal prompting from IP. The return to the assigned altitude was slow and a residual error was carried into the next maneuver.
texts.2: SP was late in adding back pressure at turn entry, so altitude decayed about 220 feet below the assigned value. SP identified the deviation on the altimeter and VSI and flew the aircraft back to the assigned altitude without any intervention by IP. The excursion remained between the 150 and 300 foot bands, but the correction should have been started earlier.
texts.3: SP held the assigned altitude within 100 feet during straight and level flight and in turns up to 60 degrees of bank. Pitch corrections were small, applied promptly and completed without over-controlling. Every deviation was detected on the altimeter and removed immediately.
texts.4: SP maintained the assigned altitude within about 30 feet throughout, with the altimeter needle essentially steady through turn entries and rollouts. Pitch was set by attitude and confirmed on the instruments, so nothing more than a light control pressure was ever required.
texts.marginal: SP remained inside the altitude standard, but the deviations clustered near 140 feet and were consistently low during the turns. Each correction was effective yet started later than required and needed more elevator than a timely input would have. SP is expected to anticipate the pitch requirement at turn entry so that the altitude trace tightens over the next sorties.

texts.0: SP, due to power lever movements made by feel and not verified against the airspeed indicator, did not hold the briefed airspeed in straight and level flight and in the turns. Airspeed diverged by about 35 knots, far beyond the 20 knot limit, and continued to build while the pitch attitude was left unchanged. IP had to reset the power and re-establish the briefed airspeed.
texts.1: SP set an approximate power setting and did not refine it against the airspeed indication as the maneuver progressed. The airspeed deviation reached 20 knots, at the limit of the standard, and was reduced only after IP called the value verbally. The recovery to the briefed airspeed was late and the power setting kept oscillating afterwards.
texts.2: SP did not add power at the entry to the turn, so the airspeed decayed about 15 knots below the briefed value. SP detected the trend on the airspeed indicator and restored the briefed airspeed with a smooth power correction and no IP input. The deviation stayed between the 10 and 20 knot bands, but a leading power correction would have prevented it.
texts.3: SP held the briefed airspeed within 8 knots through all flight phases and maneuvers. Power was set to a known value and then adjusted in small increments against the indication. Deviations were recognized early and removed without any change of pitch attitude being required.
texts.4: SP maintained the briefed airspeed within about 3 knots throughout, including through turn entries and rollouts. Power was led rather than chased, so the airspeed indication remained essentially fixed on the target value.
texts.marginal: SP stayed inside the airspeed standard, but the deviations repeatedly sat close to 10 knots and always in the slow direction during turns. Corrections were made without prompting yet each of them followed the deviation instead of anticipating it. SP is expected to lead the power requirement at maneuver entry so that airspeed dispersion narrows on the following flights.

texts.0: SP, due to no lead point computed for the rollout and no reference to the heading indicator during the turn, did not roll out on the assigned exit heading. The aircraft passed the target heading by about 20 degrees, twice the 10 degree limit, and SP started a reversal that overshot again in the opposite direction. IP had to take the controls to stop the wandering and establish the assigned heading.
texts.1: SP began the rollout without any lead and did not check the heading indicator until the wings were already level. The exit heading error reached 10 degrees, at the limit of the standard, and was corrected only after IP stated the assigned heading. The subsequent correction was flown slowly and the aircraft settled on heading well after the maneuver had ended.
texts.2: SP used an insufficient rollout lead for the bank angle flown and passed the assigned exit heading by about 8 degrees. SP recognized the error immediately on the heading indicator and returned to the assigned heading with a smooth, correctly sized turn and no IP input. The result stayed between the 5 and 10 degree bands, but the lead point should have matched the bank angle.
texts.3: SP rolled out within 4 degrees of the assigned exit heading on each turn. The rollout lead was matched to the bank angle and the heading indicator was checked before the wings reached level. Any residual error was removed at once with a small, controlled correction.
texts.4: SP rolled out on the assigned exit heading within about 1 degree on every turn, with the rollout rate matched to the bank angle. No secondary correction was needed after the wings were level.
texts.marginal: SP met the exit heading standard, but the rollouts were consistently about 5 degrees past the assigned heading and always in the same direction. The errors were self-corrected, yet the pattern shows a fixed rollout lead applied regardless of bank angle. SP is expected to scale the lead point to the bank angle and rate of turn so that rollouts finish on heading without a follow-up correction.

error_modes.label: Aileron, elevator and rudder trim technique

texts.0: SP, due to a skill-based error in trim technique, flew the aircraft with continuous control pressures through the airspeed changes and left the aileron and rudder trim at the setting of the previous flight phase. The out of trim condition produced altitude excursions beyond 300 feet and heading wander beyond 10 degrees that SP did not arrest. IP had to trim the aircraft and return it to the assigned parameters.
texts.1: SP trimmed only in pitch and did not use the aileron and rudder trim after the airspeed change, so a constant lateral pressure was carried throughout. The resulting deviations reached the 300 foot and 10 degree limits and were reduced only after IP pointed out the out of trim condition verbally. SP then trimmed with repeated large inputs rather than in small steps.
texts.2: SP was late in retrimming after the power and airspeed change and held control pressures for part of the maneuver. The residual pressures allowed altitude to drift about 200 feet and the heading to wander about 7 degrees before SP recognized the condition, trimmed the aircraft in all three axes and restored the parameters without IP intervention. Trim should have followed the airspeed change rather than the deviation it caused.
texts.3: SP handled the aileron, elevator and rudder trim correctly and without difficulty across the full airspeed range and in all flight phases. Trim followed every power and configuration change, so the aircraft was flown with the controls essentially free of pressure. Parameters were kept inside the tighter tolerance bands as a direct result.
texts.4: SP trimmed the aircraft in detail in all three axes throughout the flight, retrimming ahead of each airspeed change so that no residual control pressure was ever carried. The aircraft held attitude hands-off between corrections and the trim inputs themselves were small and unnoticeable.
texts.marginal: SP trimmed the aircraft to standard but the rudder trim was consistently left slightly out after each airspeed change and was addressed only when the ball was noticed off centre. The parameters stayed inside limits, yet a small lateral pressure was carried for longer than necessary. SP is expected to trim in all three axes as part of the power change itself so that the technique becomes automatic in the coming sorties.

error_modes.label: Instrument cross-check against aircraft position in space

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention remained on a single indication, did not compare the control and performance instruments with the position of the aircraft in space. Altitude and airspeed drifted together beyond 300 feet and 20 knots without being noticed and no correction was initiated. IP had to call the aircraft state and intervene on the controls to restore the assigned parameters.
texts.1: SP checked the instruments in a fixed sequence that stopped whenever a correction was being flown, so deviations were seen only after they had developed. Altitude reached 300 feet and airspeed 20 knots, at the limits of the standard, and the scan was re-established only after IP prompted verbally. Corrections were then made one parameter at a time while the others were left unmonitored.
texts.2: SP allowed the cross-check to slow during turns and looked at the attitude indicator for longer than the scan required. Altitude and airspeed reached about 200 feet and 15 knots before SP re-established the full scan, identified the deviations and corrected them in time and without IP intervention. The scan should have kept pace with the rate of change of the maneuver.
texts.3: SP continuously checked the indications of the control and performance instruments and compared them with the position of the aircraft in space. Deviations were detected while still small and the corresponding corrections were applied at once, keeping all parameters inside the tighter bands. The scan rate was adapted to the flight phase and to the duration of each maneuver.
texts.4: SP maintained a complete and evenly distributed cross-check throughout the flight, matching the scan rate to the rate of change of the aircraft state. Deviations were identified at the point of onset, so corrections remained at the level of light control pressures and no parameter was ever allowed to develop an error.
texts.marginal: SP kept the cross-check within standard, but it narrowed each time a correction was in progress and the heading indicator was the instrument most often left out. All parameters stayed inside limits, yet several deviations were caught later than an even scan would have allowed. SP is expected to keep the scan running through the correction itself and to include every performance instrument in the coming flights.

error_modes.label: Smooth and positive aircraft control and sizing of corrections

texts.0: SP, due to control inputs applied in abrupt steps instead of smooth pressures, did not maintain positive and smooth aircraft control for the flight conditions of the sortie. Each oversized correction produced a deviation in the opposite direction and the resulting oscillation exceeded 300 feet in altitude and 20 knots in airspeed. IP had to take the controls to damp the oscillation and stabilize the aircraft.
texts.1: SP over-controlled in pitch and roll and chased the indications rather than setting an attitude and allowing it to take effect. The oscillations reached the 300 foot and 20 knot limits and were damped only after IP verbally directed a reduction of the input size. Control of the aircraft remained coarse for the rest of the maneuver sequence.
texts.2: SP applied corrections larger than the deviations required, so each one had to be reversed before the parameter settled. Altitude and airspeed swung to about 200 feet and 15 knots before SP reduced the size of the inputs, flew smooth pressures and stabilized the aircraft without IP intervention. Corrections should have been matched to the size of the deviation from the start.
texts.3: SP maintained positive and smooth aircraft control throughout, taking into account the flight conditions of the sortie. Corrections were sized to the deviation and applied as pressures rather than movements, so no parameter overshot in the opposite direction. The aircraft was flown steadily through entries, turns and rollouts.
texts.4: SP flew the aircraft with smooth, positive and precisely sized control inputs in every phase, so that corrections were barely perceptible and no parameter ever overshot. Attitude was set once and adjusted only by light pressures, and the aircraft remained steady throughout the sortie.
texts.marginal: SP maintained control within standard, but the first correction after each maneuver entry was consistently larger than needed and had to be partly reversed. Nothing exceeded the tolerances, yet the technique produced small oscillations that a smoother input would have avoided. SP is expected to set the attitude and let it take effect before adding further input, so that the corrections become smoother over the next flights.

error_modes.label: Handling and knowledge of cockpit levers and switches

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient knowledge of the position and use of the cockpit levers and switches, searched the panels for the required control and selected an adjacent switch instead. The heads-down time and the incorrect selection left the aircraft unmonitored and the parameters passed 300 feet and 20 knots. IP had to identify the correct control and fly the aircraft while the selection was corrected.
texts.1: SP located the required levers and switches only with hesitation and confirmed each position by looking at it for an extended period. The aircraft was left unmonitored during those periods and the deviations reached the 300 foot and 20 knot limits, being corrected only after IP prompted verbally. One selection was made in the wrong sequence and had to be repeated.
texts.2: SP was slow in reaching two cockpit selections and interrupted the scan while making them, so altitude drifted about 200 feet before the deviation was noticed. SP completed the selections correctly, re-established the scan and restored the parameters in time and without IP intervention. Familiarity with the switch positions should have kept the heads-down time shorter.
texts.3: SP used all aircraft levers and switches with ease, without difficulty and without any faulty selection. Each control was found and set by position without a prolonged search, so the instrument scan was not interrupted. SP demonstrated knowledge of the position and use of every control required for the sortie.
texts.4: SP operated all levers and switches accurately by position and without looking for them, so the flow was uninterrupted and the scan was never broken. Knowledge of the position and use of the cockpit controls was complete and every selection was correct at first attempt.
texts.marginal: SP handled the cockpit controls within standard, but two selections on the right console required a deliberate look before being made. No faulty selection resulted and the parameters were held, yet the associated heads-down time was longer than the flow allows. SP is expected to build the switch positions into muscle memory through cockpit familiarization so that selections are made without interrupting the scan.

error_modes.label: Execution of actions and checks per Flight Manual, SOP and Local Area Procedures

texts.0: SP, due to distraction by a secondary cockpit task during a critical phase of flight, did not execute the actions and checks in accordance with the Flight Manual, Standard Operating Procedures and Local Area Procedures. Items of the flow were skipped and the remaining ones were performed out of sequence, so the aircraft was flown in a configuration that had not been verified. IP had to direct the omitted items and take the controls while the checks were completed.
texts.1: SP interrupted a check to respond to a radio call and did not return to the point of interruption, leaving one item unaccomplished. The omission was detected and completed only after IP verbally directed it, and the associated attention shift let the parameters reach the 300 foot and 20 knot limits. The remaining checks were then rushed rather than flown in the published order.
texts.2: SP was distracted by a secondary task and delayed the start of a required check, then performed it while the maneuver was already in progress. Altitude drifted about 200 feet during the check before SP recognized the deviation, completed all items in the published sequence and restored the parameters without IP intervention. The check should have been completed before the maneuver was entered.
texts.3: SP executed all actions and checks in accordance with the Flight Manual, Standard Operating Procedures and Local Area Procedures and skipped no procedure. Each check was completed at the correct point in the sortie and without interrupting the control of the aircraft. Secondary tasks were shed while the checks were being flown.
texts.4: SP completed every action and check exactly as published and at the correct point of the profile, with no item omitted and no sequence altered. Aircraft control and the instrument scan were fully maintained throughout each check, and secondary tasks were deferred until the flow was complete.
texts.marginal: SP followed the published procedures without omission, but two checks were begun later than the profile requires and were completed close to the maneuver entry. Nothing was skipped and the parameters were held, yet the compressed timing left no margin had a distraction occurred. SP is expected to start each check at its planned point so that the sequence is unhurried on the following sorties.

error_modes.label: Operational limits and VFR cloud clearance

texts.0: SP, due to the aircraft state being flown without reference to the published limitations, did not keep the aircraft within operational limits and did not preserve the distance from clouds required to remain VFR. The airspeed was allowed to build past the limit for the configuration and the aircraft was flown into the cloud clearance margin during the turn. IP had to take the controls to reduce the airspeed and reposition the aircraft clear of cloud.
texts.1: SP approached the published limit for the configuration and let the aircraft close on the cloud base while continuing the maneuver. Both conditions were corrected only after IP stated them verbally, and the associated attention shift left altitude at the 300 foot limit. The recovery to a compliant position was slow and the margins remained small afterwards.
texts.2: SP allowed the airspeed to move toward the published limit during the descending turn and did not plan the maneuver against the cloud base. SP recognized both conditions before any limit was reached, reduced power and repositioned the aircraft to preserve the required cloud clearance without IP intervention. The maneuver should have been positioned against the weather before it was entered.
texts.3: SP maintained the aircraft within operational limits at all times and preserved the distance from clouds required to remain VFR throughout the flight. Maneuvers were positioned against the cloud base before entry and the airspeed and bank were kept clear of the published limitations. No margin was reduced at any point of the sortie.
texts.4: SP kept the aircraft comfortably inside every operational limit and maintained generous VFR cloud clearance throughout, repositioning the working area in advance as the cloud base changed. Each maneuver was planned so that no limit or clearance margin was ever approached.
texts.marginal: SP remained within operational limits and VFR cloud clearance, but the working altitude was selected close to the cloud base and the margin had to be protected by shortening two maneuvers. No limit or clearance was infringed, yet the initial positioning left little room for the developing weather. SP is expected to select the working block against the observed cloud base so that the margins are built in from the start.

error_modes.label: Detection of erroneous instrument indications and notification of IP

texts.0: SP, due to each instrument being read in isolation and never cross-referenced against the others, did not locate the erroneous indication that was present during the maneuver. SP flew the aircraft on the faulty reading, did not inform IP and executed no corresponding procedure, so the parameters diverged beyond 300 feet and 20 knots. IP had to identify the erroneous instrument and take the controls.
texts.1: SP noticed that one indication did not agree with the aircraft state but continued the maneuver without resolving the disagreement. The erroneous reading was identified and reported to IP only after a verbal prompt, and the corresponding procedure was started late. During that period the deviations reached the 300 foot and 20 knot limits of the standard.
texts.2: SP was slow to compare the suspect indication against the other instruments and continued to fly on it for part of the maneuver, allowing about a 200 foot altitude drift. SP then identified the erroneous reading, informed IP and executed the corresponding procedure in time and without IP intervention. The cross-reference should have been made as soon as the indication disagreed with the aircraft state.
texts.3: SP timely located the erroneous instrument reading, informed IP and executed the corresponding procedure. The disagreement was resolved against the remaining control and performance instruments while aircraft control and the assigned parameters were fully maintained. The maneuver was continued on valid references.
texts.4: SP identified the erroneous indication at the moment it appeared, cross-referenced it against the remaining instruments, informed IP in clear terms and executed the corresponding procedure without any interruption of aircraft control. All parameters were held precisely throughout the sequence.
texts.marginal: SP detected the erroneous indication and reported it to IP within standard, but the cross-reference against the other instruments took longer than the situation allowed and the report was made after the maneuver had ended. Aircraft control was maintained and the correct procedure was applied, yet the detection was later than a full scan would have produced. SP is expected to resolve any disagreement between instruments as soon as it appears and to report it immediately in the coming flights.

error_modes.label: Rudder use with aileron to counter adverse yaw

texts.0: SP, due to aileron pressure applied without simultaneous rudder in the same direction, let adverse yaw swing the nose opposite the direction of every roll. The ball was hard over through each entry and rollout, the turns started with the nose off the intended arc, exit headings passed the assigned value by more than 10 degrees and altitude broke 300 feet. IP had to take the controls to coordinate the aircraft and re-establish the assigned parameters.
texts.1: SP applied rudder only after the bank was already established, so the nose yawed away from the direction of the roll at every entry. The uncoordinated entries drove the exit heading error to 10 degrees, at the limit of the standard, and were corrected only after repeated calls from IP to apply rudder together with aileron. The same omission was repeated on the rollouts, where the aileron drag effect was left uncountered.
texts.2: SP applied rudder with the aileron at turn entry but released it before the bank stopped changing, so a residual adverse yaw appeared on each rollout. The nose swung about 8 degrees off the intended heading and the ball came off centre, and SP recognized the yaw, added rudder in the direction of the aileron pressure and finished inside the limits without any IP input. Rudder pressure should have been held for as long as the bank was changing.
texts.3: SP applied aileron and rudder simultaneously in the direction of the turn and held rudder pressure for as long as the bank was changing, on entries as well as on rollouts. Adverse yaw was contained, the turn and slip indicator stayed close to centre and exit headings were made within 5 degrees.
texts.4: SP coordinated aileron and rudder so precisely that the nose tracked along the intended arc with no perceptible yaw at any roll entry or rollout. The ball remained centred throughout and every exit heading was made within about 1 degree with no follow-up correction.
texts.marginal: SP countered adverse yaw within standard, but rudder pressure was consistently lighter on the rollouts than on the entries and the ball drifted slightly off centre each time the wings came level. Headings stayed inside 5 degrees, yet the pattern shows aileron drag being treated as an entry-only effect. SP is expected to use rudder in the same direction as the aileron pressure on the rollout as well as on the entry so that coordination becomes uniform.

error_modes.label: Matching bank angle to turn rate (skid and slip)

texts.0: SP, due to excessive bottom rudder held against insufficient bank angle in relation to the turn rate, kept the aircraft in a continuous skid through the turns and reversed it into a slip whenever the rudder was released. The flight path was no longer a true circle, airspeed varied with every uncoordinated input and exit heading and altitude ran beyond 10 degrees and 300 feet. IP had to take the controls to centre the ball and restore coordinated flight, since the skid was being carried at slow airspeed.
texts.1: SP flew the turns with insufficient bank angle in relation to the turn rate and made up the difference with bottom rudder, so the aircraft was skidding for most of each turn. The resulting variation in the flight path drove the exit heading error to 10 degrees, at the limit of the standard, and the ball was centred only after direct instruction from IP. SP did not associate the ball deflection with the mismatch between bank angle and turn rate.
texts.2: SP held slightly too much bank angle for the turn rate in the steeper turns, so the aircraft slipped and the ball displaced to the inside of the turn. The uncoordinated flight path cost about 200 feet of altitude before SP stepped on the ball, matched the bank to the turn rate and returned to the assigned altitude without IP intervention. The turn and slip indicator should have been in the crosscheck from the entry.
texts.3: SP matched the bank angle to the turn rate in shallow and steep turns alike and kept the ball centred with rudder pressure rather than with bank. No skid or slip developed, the flight path stayed circular, altitude was held within 100 feet and exit headings within 5 degrees.
texts.4: SP flew every turn in coordinated flight with the ball centred from entry to rollout and the bank angle matched to the turn rate throughout. The flight path remained a true circle, airspeed was constant and nothing more than a light rudder pressure was ever required.
texts.marginal: SP kept the turns coordinated within standard, but a small amount of bottom rudder was carried in the 45 to 60 degree bank turns and the ball sat just outside centre for several seconds at a time. Altitude and heading stayed inside the limits, yet the developing skid was recognized only when it was pointed out on the instrument. SP is expected to set the bank angle for the desired turn rate first and use rudder solely to centre the ball on the coming sorties.

error_modes.label: Rudder compensation for slipstream effect and torque during power changes

texts.0: SP, due to PCL movements made without the matching rudder input, let the corkscrew slipstream and torque yaw and roll the aircraft left on every power increase and right on every power reduction. The PCL was moved abruptly and through large travel, so the nose swung across the horizon uncontrolled and heading and altitude passed 10 degrees and 300 feet. IP had to take the controls to stop the yaw and re-establish coordinated flight.
texts.1: SP moved the right foot forward only after the yaw had already developed, so each power increase started with the nose swinging left across the horizon. The heading error reached 10 degrees, at the limit of the standard, and coordinated flight was restored only after IP called for rudder with every PCL movement. The same omission produced an uncontrolled right swing on the power reductions.
texts.2: SP applied right rudder with the power increase but not in proportion to the amount and rate of PCL movement, so the nose swung about 8 degrees left before it was stopped. SP saw the swing against the horizon, added the required rudder and returned to the assigned heading in time and without IP intervention. The rudder input should have been sized to the rate of PCL movement from the start.
texts.3: SP moved the right foot forward as the PCL was advanced and applied left rudder on the power reductions, so the nose was kept from swinging in either direction. Heading was held within 5 degrees through the power changes and the ball stayed close to centre.
texts.4: SP matched the amount and rate of rudder to the amount and rate of PCL movement so precisely that the nose did not move against the horizon during any power change. Heading was held within about 1 degree, the aircraft stayed coordinated and no secondary correction followed any power adjustment.
texts.marginal: SP countered the slipstream and torque effects within standard, but rudder was slightly under-applied on the larger power increases and the nose crept left before being stopped. Heading stayed inside 5 degrees and the corrections were effective, yet the input was sized for an average power change rather than the one being made. SP is expected to scale the rudder to the amount and rate of PCL movement so that the nose stays fixed on the reference point.

error_modes.label: Abrupt corrections coupling into gyroscopic precession

texts.0: SP, due to deviations in pitch, bank and yaw being corrected abruptly instead of with smooth pressures, fed the propeller gyroscopic precession into every input, so each force acted in a plane 90 degrees from the one in which it was applied. A yaw correction to the left pitched the nose up, the following pitch input yawed the aircraft again and the coupled oscillation carried altitude beyond 300 feet and airspeed beyond 20 knots. IP had to take the controls to damp the oscillation and stabilize the aircraft.
texts.1: SP corrected each deviation with a rapid input, so a nose-down pitch correction developed a left yaw and heading and altitude then had to be chased in turn. The excursions reached the 300 foot and 10 degree limits of the standard and settled only after IP repeatedly directed slower and smoother inputs. SP continued to treat each axis as independent of the others.
texts.2: SP made two pitch corrections at a higher rate of movement than the deviation required, and the resulting yaw reaction moved the heading about 8 degrees off the assigned value. SP recognized that the abrupt input had produced the secondary reaction, reduced the rate of the following corrections and recovered the parameters without IP intervention. Increased rates of movement about the pitch and yaw axes increase the precession effect.
texts.3: SP corrected deviations in pitch, bank and yaw with smooth inputs at a controlled rate, so no secondary precession reaction was generated in the adjacent axis. Altitude stayed within 100 feet and heading within 5 degrees, and no correction had to be followed by a second one in another axis.
texts.4: SP applied every correction so smoothly that the large high rpm propeller produced no perceptible precession reaction in any axis. Each deviation was removed with a single input and the aircraft remained steady, with altitude within about 30 feet and heading essentially fixed.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft inside the tolerances, but the first correction after each maneuver entry was applied at a rate that produced a small reaction in the adjacent axis and had to be tidied up afterwards. Nothing exceeded the limits, yet the pattern shows the precession effect being absorbed after the fact instead of being avoided. SP is expected to reduce the rate of movement about the pitch and yaw axes so that corrections stop generating work in the other axes.

error_modes.label: Composite flight crosscheck distribution between outside and inside references

texts.0: SP, due to over-reliance upon instrumentation to maintain aircraft attitude, set and held the attitude inside the cockpit instead of positioning the nose and wings in relation to the horizon. The head-down time far exceeded the twenty per cent that inside references should receive in clear conditions, clearing for other aircraft effectively stopped and the parameters still diverged beyond 300 feet and 20 knots. IP had to take the controls and direct SP back onto outside references.
texts.1: SP flew every attitude on the flight instruments and used the horizon only after a deviation had already appeared. The excessive head-down time impeded the ability to observe other aircraft and hazards, and the altitude excursions reached the 300 foot limit of the standard, recovering only after repeated calls from IP to look outside. The eighty per cent outside and twenty per cent inside distribution was not applied at any point of the sortie.
texts.2: SP established the attitude against the horizon but then held the crosscheck inside the cockpit while the correction took effect, losing the distribution between outside and inside references for several seconds at a time. Altitude drifted about 200 feet before SP returned to the outside picture, resumed clearing and recovered the parameters without IP intervention. The instruments should have been used to confirm the attitude, not to fly it.
texts.3: SP established and maintained each attitude by positioning the nose and wings in relation to the horizon and crosschecked the flight instruments for the small changes not readily noticed outside. The distribution stayed close to eighty per cent outside and twenty per cent inside, clearing was continuous and altitude was held within 100 feet.
texts.4: SP flew the whole profile on outside references, with the instruments used only to confirm what the horizon already showed. Clearing was vigilant and uninterrupted, no single cue was allowed to dominate the crosscheck and every parameter was held with deviations of no practical size.
texts.marginal: SP kept the composite crosscheck within standard, but the share of time spent inside the cockpit grew during the turns and the horizon was used mainly to verify the instrument picture. All parameters stayed inside the limits and clearing continued, yet the head-down time in the steeper turns was longer than the clear conditions justified. SP is expected to hold the attitude on the horizon and reserve the instruments for confirmation so that the distribution stays near eighty per cent outside.

error_modes.label: Correction of nose-low and nose-high attitudes in steep turns

texts.0: SP, due to the steep turn being treated as a different maneuver rather than one in which the same aerodynamic effects are more pronounced, answered the nose dropping in the 60 degree bank turn with back stick pressure alone and left the bank angle untouched. The added back pressure tightened the turn instead of raising the nose, so the descent accelerated beyond 300 feet and airspeed built beyond 20 knots. IP had to take the controls, reduce the angle of bank and recover the aircraft to the assigned altitude.
texts.1: SP allowed the nose to go low in the steep turns and attempted to recover it with elevator while holding the bank at 60 degrees. The altitude loss reached the 300 foot limit of the standard and was arrested only after IP called for the angle of bank to be reduced first. The relationship between angle of bank, back pressure and pitch attitude was not applied.
texts.2: SP was late in detecting the nose-low attitude in the steep turn because the VSI was not being crosschecked, and about 200 feet were lost before the correction began. SP then reduced the angle of bank with coordinated aileron and rudder, adjusted back pressure to raise the nose and re-established the desired bank without IP intervention. The correction was made in the right order but should have started earlier.
texts.3: SP detected nose-low and nose-high attitudes in the steep turns from the VSI and corrected them by adjusting the angle of bank with coordinated aileron and rudder while simultaneously adjusting back pressure. The desired angle of bank was re-established once the attitude was recovered and altitude stayed within 100 feet.
texts.4: SP flew shallow and steep turns with the same technique, differing only in the amount of back stick pressure and power required, so the pitch attitude never departed from the desired picture. No nose-low or nose-high correction was needed and altitude and airspeed were held with negligible deviation throughout.
texts.marginal: SP corrected the steep turn attitudes within standard, but the first response was always a small increase in back pressure and the angle of bank was adjusted only when that failed to raise the nose. Altitude stayed inside the limits and every turn was recovered, yet the sequence cost more altitude than a bank adjustment would have. SP is expected to reduce the angle of bank and adjust back pressure together, then re-establish the desired bank.

error_modes.label: Control stick grip and inadvertent stick force from the weight of the arm

texts.0: SP, due to the control stick being gripped with the whole hand and carrying the weight of the arm, applied force to the control stick inadvertently and never felt the out-of-trim condition through the fingertips. The unnoticed pressure held the aircraft off the trimmed attitude, altitude wandered beyond 300 feet and airspeed followed beyond 20 knots without the source being identified. IP had to take the controls and demonstrate a light fingertip touch before the aircraft could be flown on attitude again.
texts.1: SP flew with a tight grip and an unsupported arm, so a continuous inadvertent pressure was carried on the control stick during straight and level flight. The altitude deviation reached the 300 foot limit of the standard and the cause was found only after IP instructed SP to rest the forearm on the thigh and release the stick. The aircraft was in fact correctly trimmed and the deviation came from the arm alone.
texts.2: SP let the arm rest on the control stick during the level segments and added an unintended nose-down pressure, so altitude decayed about 200 feet. SP noticed that the aircraft would not hold the trimmed attitude, supported the forearm on the thigh, loosened the grip and returned to the assigned altitude without IP intervention. The touch should have been light enough to feel the trim state from the start.
texts.3: SP flew with a firm but light touch and a supported forearm, so no inadvertent stick force was applied during straight and level flight. Slight out-of-trim conditions were felt through the fingertips and removed with trim, and altitude was held within 100 feet.
texts.4: SP flew the cruise segments on fingertips alone with the forearm supported, so the most minute changes of trim were felt as soon as they appeared. The aircraft held the trimmed attitude essentially hands-off and altitude and airspeed remained steady with negligible deviation.
texts.marginal: SP held the parameters within standard, but the grip tightened whenever workload increased and a small unintended pressure appeared on the control stick during the busier segments. Nothing exceeded the tolerances, yet the feedback on trim was lost exactly when it was most needed. SP is expected to keep the forearm supported and the touch light so that out-of-trim conditions continue to be felt under higher workload.

error_modes.label: Level-off lead point taken from the rate of climb

texts.0: SP, due to the level-off being started at the assigned altitude with no lead point taken from the rate of climb, flew the aircraft through the level-off altitude with the climb attitude still set. The overshoot exceeded 300 feet, the recovery was then made with a large nose-down input and airspeed ran beyond 20 knots as the nose was pushed over. IP had to take the controls to capture the assigned altitude and set the level flight attitude.
texts.1: SP used the same lead point regardless of the rate of climb and began the level-off far too late while climbing at about 2000 feet per minute. The overshoot reached 300 feet, at the limit of the standard, and the altitude was recaptured only after IP directed the pitch change and the power reduction. Airspeed was left to chase the attitude throughout the level-off.
texts.2: SP started the level-off with a lead point smaller than ten per cent of the rate shown on the VSI, so the aircraft passed about 200 feet above the assigned altitude. SP smoothly lowered the nose, adjusted the PCL to the desired airspeed and returned to the altitude in time and without IP intervention. The lead point should have been read from the VSI rather than assumed.
texts.3: SP took a lead point of approximately ten per cent of the rate shown on the VSI, smoothly lowered the nose at that point and adjusted the PCL to obtain the desired airspeed. The level-off was captured within 100 feet of the assigned altitude and the aircraft was trimmed as the airspeed settled.
texts.4: SP scaled the level-off lead point to the rate of climb on every level-off, so the aircraft arrived at the assigned altitude with the level flight attitude already set. Altitude was captured within about 30 feet, the airspeed settled on the desired value with a single power adjustment and the aircraft was trimmed immediately.
texts.marginal: SP levelled off within standard, but the lead point was slightly short at the higher rates of climb and the aircraft consistently arrived about 120 feet high before settling. Every capture was made and no limit was approached, yet each one required a second nose-down correction. SP is expected to read the VSI before each level-off and use a lead point of approximately ten per cent of the indicated rate.
